posts.post_text: We banned ChatGPT in our analytics department last month. Not because AI is bad — because nobody could explain where the numbers came from. When a regulator asks 'how did you arrive at this figure?' and the answer is 'GPT said so', you've got a compliance problem. The AI trust gap is real and growing.
posts.angle: High-scoring compliance pain post with three senior ICP prospects engaging — validate the 'explainability' problem with a specific observation, position auditability as the real unlock, no pitch
posts.draft_comment: The ban makes complete sense. 'GPT said so' isn't an audit trail, it's a liability. The teams I see actually getting comfortable with AI in regulated contexts aren't the ones who found better AI — they're the ones who stopped treating explainability as a nice-to-have and built it in from the start. I wonder how many tools out there even make that possible.

posts.post_text: We spent 18 months building a Power BI dashboard that our finance team refuses to use. They still export everything to Excel and email it around. The building part was easy. Getting people to actually trust the numbers enough to quote them in a board meeting? That's the real challenge nobody talks about. Anyone else hit this wall?
posts.angle: ICP prospect COO at 140-person consulting firm hitting the trust-not-tools wall — validate the real problem (credibility, not UX) and leave her thinking
posts.draft_comment: The dashboard was never the problem. It's that the moment a number gets challenged in a board meeting and nobody can explain where it came from, everyone quietly goes back to the spreadsheet they trust. 18 months of build can unravel in one awkward silence. What was the moment yours lost the room?

posts.post_text: Unpopular opinion: most operational dashboards are vanity projects. We had 47 KPIs on our ops dashboard. Nobody looked at it. Cut it to 5 metrics that actually drive decisions. Usage went from 10% to 85%. The problem with BI isn't the tools — it's that we measure everything and understand nothing.
posts.angle: ICP prospect (Director of Operations at Summit Group) engaging with a post about dashboard bloat — validate the 47-to-5 insight, add the 'why dashboards get bloated in the first place' layer, no pitch
posts.draft_comment: 47 KPIs is usually a political problem dressed up as a measurement problem — every team wants their metric on the board, so nobody says no. The dashboards that actually get used are the ones where someone had the nerve to make that call early. Curious what the pushback was like when you cut it down to 5 — because that conversation is usually the hardest part.

posts.post_text: Hot take: self-service BI is a myth. We gave everyone Power BI licenses and what happened? 200 reports, zero consistency, three different definitions of 'revenue'. The promise of democratising data is great until you realise nobody agrees on what the data means. Build vs buy isn't the question — it's 'who owns the truth?'
posts.angle: ICP prospect (Innovation Director at NorthStar Retail) engaging with a post about self-service BI chaos — validate the 'who owns truth' pain, add the governance-over-tooling insight, no pitch
posts.draft_comment: The three definitions of revenue thing is so common it's almost a rite of passage. Most teams go straight to 'better tooling' but the actual problem is that nobody decided who gets to define the terms before the licenses went out. Power BI didn't create the disagreement — it just made it visible at scale. Makes you wonder if the real work was always the conversation, not the dashboard.

posts.post_text: AI hallucinations in analytics are a security issue, not just an accuracy issue. If your AI tool generates a financial report with hallucinated numbers and someone makes a decision based on it, that's not a bug — it's a material risk. We need to start treating AI outputs with the same scrutiny as we treat user inputs.
posts.angle: CISO at Fortis raising AI hallucinations as a security risk with a CEO prospect engaging — validate the framing, add the trust-layer insight, no pitch
posts.draft_comment: The security framing here is underrated. Most teams I talk to are still treating hallucinated outputs as a QA problem — something to catch after the fact. But if a fabricated number clears review and lands in a board deck, the damage is done before anyone even knows to look. How many orgs have actually mapped AI-generated analytics outputs to their existing data governance controls — or is that gap still mostly invisible?

posts.post_text: Had a fascinating conversation with a client yesterday. They spent £200k on a BI platform and the only person who can use it is the one who built it. Self-service my arse. The gap between what vendors promise and what actually happens in a 50-person company is enormous. When will the industry admit that most BI tools are built for data teams, not business teams?
posts.angle: CEO of 65-person advisory firm validating mid-market BI failure with ICP prospect (COO at Sterling Consulting) engaging — confirm the structural problem, add the 'built for builders not users' insight, no pitch
posts.draft_comment: The £200k isn't even the painful part — it's the 18 months of goodwill burned waiting for something that was supposed to make everyone independent but made one person indispensable instead. Most of these tools are genuinely brilliant if you already think in data models. But that's not Helen in ops, that's not the account director pulling a client report at 8pm. The vendors know this too, they just haven't figured out how to sell 'actually simple' as a feature yet.

posts.post_text: Just had our quarterly review and the CFO asked why the numbers in our BI dashboard don't match the numbers in the ERP. Turns out three different teams were applying different filters to the same dataset. AI won't fix this. Culture will. But nobody wants to hear that.
posts.angle: Commercial Director at a likely mid-market manufacturer hitting the classic 'whose numbers are right?' problem — validate the culture diagnosis but add the missing layer about definitions, not just filters
posts.draft_comment: Three teams, three filter sets, one awkward CFO question — that's not really a culture problem, it's a definitions problem that culture gets blamed for. Nobody agreed upfront what 'quarterly revenue' actually means before they all went off and built their own version of it. The tool didn't cause that, but a better-designed tool probably should have forced the conversation earlier. Did anyone in that review actually agree on the right number by the end, or just agree to fix it later?

posts.post_text: Rolled out Copilot to 500 users last quarter. Usage after 90 days? 12%. The problem isn't the tool — it's that nobody knows what to ask it. We're essentially paying for a very expensive autocomplete. Shadow AI is the real story here — people are using ChatGPT on their phones because Copilot is too locked down.
posts.angle: IT Director surfacing the real adoption failure mode (nobody knows what to ask) — validate the prompt literacy problem and add the shadow AI insight that the locked-down tools lose to permissionless ones every time
posts.draft_comment: The 12% number is almost always a prompt literacy problem, not a product problem — people don't know what good looks like so they stop trying. And the shadow AI thing is the part that should keep IT directors up at night, because the workaround is already happening, just outside your visibility. The irony is that the more locked-down you make the sanctioned tool, the faster people route around it. What would it look like if the tool came with the questions pre-loaded instead of waiting for users to invent them?
